[Proverbs] [30]:[30] the lion, mightiest among beasts, who retreats before nothing;
[Proverbs] [30]:[31] the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king at the head of his troops.
[Proverbs] [30]:[32] If you have been foolish and exalted yourself, or if you have schemed—put your hand over your mouth.
[Proverbs] [30]:[33] For as churning milk produces butter and twisting the nose produces blood, so stirring up anger produces strife.
[Proverbs] [31]:[1] The words of Lemuel, king of Massa, which his mother taught him:
[Proverbs] [31]:[2] What shall I say, my son? What, son of my womb? What, son of my vows?
[Proverbs] [31]:[3] Do not give your strength to women, nor your ways to those who ruin kings.
[Proverbs] [31]:[4] It is not for kings, Lemuel—not for kings to drink wine, nor for rulers to crave strong drink,
[Proverbs] [31]:[5] lest they drink and forget the law, and pervert the justice due to all the afflicted.
[Proverbs] [31]:[6] Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress.
[Proverbs] [31]:[7] Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their misery no more.
[Proverbs] [31]:[8] Open your mouth for the one who cannot speak, for the rights of all the destitute.
[Proverbs] [31]:[9] Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the cause of the poor and needy.
[Proverbs] [31]:[10] A wife of noble character—who can find her? She is worth far more than pearls.
[Proverbs] [31]:[11] Her husband's heart trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value.
[Proverbs] [31]:[12] She brings him good and not harm all the days of her life.
[Proverbs] [31]:[13] She seeks out wool and flax, and her hands work with delight.
[Proverbs] [31]:[14] She is like a merchant's ships, bringing her food from far away.
[Proverbs] [31]:[15] She rises while it is still night, sets food before her household, and gives portions to her servant girls.
[Proverbs] [31]:[16] She considers a field and buys it; from the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard.
[Proverbs] [31]:[17] She girds herself with strength and makes her arms strong.
[Proverbs] [31]:[18] She sees that her trading is profitable; her lamp does not go out at night.
[Proverbs] [31]:[19] She reaches out her hands to the distaff and grasps the spindle with her fingers.
[Proverbs] [31]:[20] She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out to the needy.
[Proverbs] [31]:[21] She has no fear of snow for her household, for all of them are clothed in scarlet.
[Proverbs] [31]:[22] She makes coverings for her bed; her clothing is fine linen and purple.
[Proverbs] [31]:[23] Her husband is known in the gates, where he sits among the elders of the land.
[Proverbs] [31]:[24] She makes linen garments and sells them, and supplies the merchants with sashes.
[Proverbs] [31]:[25] Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the days to come.
[Proverbs] [31]:[26] She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue.
[Proverbs] [31]:[27] She watches over the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.
[Proverbs] [31]:[28] Her children rise and call her blessed; her husband praises her as well:
[Proverbs] [31]:[29] "Many women do noble things, but you surpass them all."
[Proverbs] [31]:[30] Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
[Proverbs] [31]:[31] Give her the reward of her labor, and let her works praise her in the gates.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[1] The words of the Preacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[2] Futility of futilities, says the Preacher. Futility of futilities! Everything is futile.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[3] What does anyone gain from all the labor he toils at under the sun?
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[4] One generation goes, another comes, but the earth stands forever.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[5] The sun rises and the sun sets, then pants back to the place where it rises again.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[6] The wind blows south, then turns north; round and round it goes, and back again to where it started.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[7] All the rivers run to the sea, yet the sea is never full; to the place where the rivers flow, there they return to flow again.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[8] All things are wearisome; no one can put it into words. The eye never has enough of seeing, nor the ear its fill of hearing.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[9] What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done; there is nothing new under the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[10] Is there something of which people say, "Look, this is new"? It was here long ago, in the ages before us.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[11] No one remembers those who came first, and even those who are yet to come will not be remembered by those who follow them.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[12] I, the Preacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[13] I set my mind to search out and examine with wisdom everything done under heaven. It is a miserable task that God has given the children of Adam to occupy themselves with.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[14] I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and it is all futile, a chasing after the wind.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[15] What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is missing cannot be counted. Footnote: Literally "a lack cannot be numbered" — what is not there cannot be added to the count.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[16] I said to myself: Look, I have grown great and gained more wisdom than anyone who ruled Jerusalem before me; my mind has taken in much wisdom and knowledge.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[17] So I set my mind to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly as well. And I came to know that this too is a chasing after the wind.
[Ecclesiastes] [1]:[18] For with much wisdom comes much grief, and the more knowledge, the more sorrow.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[1] I said to myself, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good." But look—this too is a fleeting breath.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[2] Of laughter I said, "It is madness," and of pleasure, "What does it accomplish?"
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[3] I explored in my heart how to cheer my body with wine—my mind still guiding me with wisdom—and how to lay hold of folly, until I might see what is good for people to do under heaven during the few days of their lives.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[4] I undertook great works: I built houses for myself and planted vineyards for myself.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[5] I made gardens and parks for myself and planted in them every kind of fruit tree.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[6] I made reservoirs for myself, to water a grove of growing trees.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[7] I bought male and female slaves, and I had servants born in my house. I also owned more herds and flocks than anyone in Jerusalem before me.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[8] I amassed silver and gold for myself, the treasure of kings and provinces. I acquired male and female singers, and the delights of men—a harem.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[9] So I became great, surpassing everyone in Jerusalem before me. And still my wisdom stayed with me.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[10] Whatever my eyes desired I did not withhold from them; I refused my heart no pleasure. My heart found joy in all my labor, and this was my reward for all my labor.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[11] Then I turned to consider all the works my hands had done and the labor I had spent doing them, and look—it was all a fleeting breath, a chasing after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[12] Then I turned to consider wisdom, along with madness and folly. For what can the one do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[13] And I saw that wisdom surpasses folly as light surpasses darkness.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[14] The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also came to know that one and the same fate overtakes them both.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[15] So I said to myself, "The fate of the fool will overtake me as well. Why then have I been so very wise?" And I said in my heart that this too is a fleeting breath.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[16] For the wise man, like the fool, is not remembered forever; in the days to come both will be long forgotten. How is it that the wise man dies just like the fool?
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[17] So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. It is all a fleeting breath, a chasing after wind.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[18] I hated all the fruit of my labor under the sun, because I must leave it to the one who comes after me.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[19] And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will have mastery over all the fruit of my labor, into which I poured my toil and my wisdom under the sun. This too is a fleeting breath.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[20] So I turned and gave my heart over to despair concerning all the labor I had toiled at under the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[21] For here is a man whose work is done with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, and he must hand it all over as a portion to someone who never worked for it. This too is a fleeting breath, and a great evil.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[22] For what does a person get from all his labor and from the striving of his heart, as he toils under the sun?
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[23] All his days his work brings pain and grief; even at night his mind does not rest. This too is a fleeting breath.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[24] There is nothing better for a person than to eat and drink and find enjoyment in his labor. This too, I saw, comes from the hand of God.
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[25] For who can eat, and who can find enjoyment, apart from him?
[Ecclesiastes] [2]:[26] To the one who pleases him God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he gives the task of gathering and heaping up, only to hand it over to the one who pleases God. This too is a fleeting breath, a chasing after wind.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[1] For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[2] a time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what is planted;
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[3] a time to kill and a time to heal; a time to tear down and a time to build;
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[4] a time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance;
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[5] a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them; a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing;
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[6] a time to seek and a time to lose; a time to keep and a time to throw away;
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[7] a time to tear and a time to mend; a time to be silent and a time to speak;
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[8] a time to love and a time to hate; a time for war and a time for peace.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[9] What does the worker gain from all his toil?
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[10] I have seen the task God has given to the children of man to keep them occupied.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[11] He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet no one can grasp what God has done from beginning to end.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[12] I know there is nothing better for people than to rejoice and do good while they live.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[13] Also, that everyone should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his toil—this is the gift of God.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[14] I know that everything God does will endure forever; nothing can be added to it and nothing taken from it. God has done it so that people will stand in awe before him.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[15] Whatever is has already been, and what will be has been before; and God seeks out what has been driven away.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[16] And I saw something else under the sun: in the place of judgment—wickedness was there; in the place of justice—wickedness was there.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[17] I said in my heart, "God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every deed."
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[18] I said in my heart concerning the children of man: God tests them to show them that they are but animals.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[19] For the fate of man and the fate of the animal are one and the same: as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the animal, for everything is vanity.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[20] All go to one place. All came from the dust, and to the dust all return.
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[21] Who knows whether the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal goes down into the earth?
[Ecclesiastes] [3]:[22] So I saw that there is nothing better than for a person to rejoice in his work, for that is his portion. Who can bring him to see what will come after him?
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[1] Again I looked and saw all the oppression that goes on under the sun. Look at the tears of the oppressed—and no one to comfort them. Power was in the hand of their oppressors—and no one to comfort them.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[2] So I called the dead, who have already died, more fortunate than the living, who are still alive.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[3] But better off than either is the one who has never been born, who has never seen the evil that is done under the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[4] And I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from one person's envy of another. This too is vanity, a chasing after the wind.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[5] The fool folds his hands and devours his own flesh.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[6] Better a handful with quiet rest than two fists full of toil and a chasing after the wind.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[7] Again I looked, and I saw something futile under the sun:
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[8] a man all alone, with no one beside him—no son, no brother—yet there is no end to his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with wealth. "For whom am I working so hard," he asks, "and denying myself every good thing?" This too is vanity, a wretched business.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[9] Two are better than one, because together they have a good reward for their labor.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[10] If one of them falls, the other can lift him up. But pity the one who falls alone, with no one to lift him up.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[11] And if two lie down together, they keep warm; but how can one stay warm alone?
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[12] Though someone may overpower one alone, two can stand against him. And a cord of three strands is not easily broken.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[13] Better a poor but wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take warning.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[14] For the youth came out of prison to reign, though he was born poor in that very kingdom.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[15] I saw that all the living who move about under the sun sided with the young successor who took the king's place.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[16] There was no end to the people, to all those he led. Yet those who come after will take no delight in him. This too is vanity, a chasing after the wind.
[Ecclesiastes] [4]:[17] Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. Draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools, who do not even know that they are doing wrong.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[1] Do not be rash with your mouth, and do not let your heart hurry to bring out a word before God. For God is in heaven and you are on earth; therefore let your words be few.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[2] For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[3] When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, for he takes no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[4] Better not to vow at all than to vow and not fulfill it.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[5] Do not let your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say to the messenger, "It was a mistake." Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands?
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[6] For in many dreams and many words there is much emptiness. So fear God.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[7] If you see the poor oppressed in a province, and justice and right torn away, do not be astonished at the matter; for one official is watched by a higher one, and over them all are higher ones still.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[8] And the profit of a land is in every way this: a king devoted to the cultivated field.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[9] Whoever loves money is never satisfied with money, and whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with income. This too is vanity.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[10] When goods increase, so do those who eat them. And what gain has the owner, except to look at them with his eyes?
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[11] Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich man will not let him sleep.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[12] There is a grievous evil I have seen under the sun: riches hoarded by their owner to his own hurt.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[13] Those riches were lost in a bad venture, and the son he fathered was left with nothing in his hand.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[14] As he came from his mother's womb, so he goes again, naked as he came; and he can carry nothing away from his toil that he may take in his hand.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[15] This too is a grievous evil: just as he came, so he goes. What gain does he have, having toiled for the wind?
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[16] All his days he eats in darkness, with much frustration, sickness, and anger.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[17] This is what I have seen to be good: that a man should eat and drink and find enjoyment in all his toil under the sun during the few days of life God has given him, for this is his portion.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[18] Moreover, when God gives someone riches and possessions, and lets him enjoy them, take his portion, and find joy in his toil—this is a gift of God.
[Ecclesiastes] [5]:[19] For he will hardly think about the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the gladness of his heart.
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[1] There is an evil I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy upon humankind:
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[2] a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his soul desires—yet God does not let him enjoy it, and a stranger consumes it instead. This is meaningless, a grievous affliction.
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[3] A man may father a hundred children and live many years; yet however long his days may be, if his soul is not satisfied with good and he receives no burial, then I say the stillborn child is better off than he.
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[4] For it comes in emptiness and departs in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered over.
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[5] It never saw the sun, never knew a thing—yet it has more rest than he does.
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[6] Even if he lived a thousand years twice over but never enjoyed the good—do not all go to the same place?
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[7] All a person's toil is for his mouth, and still the appetite is never filled.
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[8] What advantage, then, has the wise over the fool? What does the poor man gain by knowing how to conduct himself before the living?
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[9] Better what the eyes can see than the wandering of desire. This too is meaningless, a chasing after wind.
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[10] Whatever has come to be was named long ago, and it is known that he is only a man: he cannot contend with one stronger than himself.
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[11] For there are many words, and they multiply emptiness—so what advantage is there for anyone?
[Ecclesiastes] [6]:[12] For who knows what is good for a person in life, through the numbered days of his fleeting life, which he spends like a shadow? And who can tell anyone what will come after him under the sun?
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[1] A good name is better than fine perfume, and the day of death than the day of birth.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[2] Better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting, for death is the end of everyone, and the living should take it to heart.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[3] Sorrow is better than laughter, for a sad face is good for the heart.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[4] The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[5] Better to hear the rebuke of the wise than to listen to the song of fools.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[6] For like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools. This too is vanity.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[7] Extortion makes a wise man foolish, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[8] Better the end of a matter than its beginning; better patience of spirit than pride of spirit.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[9] Do not let your spirit be quick to anger, for anger settles in the lap of fools.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[10] Do not ask, "Why were the old days better than these?" It is not from wisdom that you ask this.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[11] Wisdom is good along with an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[12] For wisdom is a shelter as money is a shelter, but the gain of knowledge is this: wisdom preserves the life of the one who has it.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[13] Consider the work of God: who can straighten what he has made crooked?
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[14] In the day of prosperity be glad, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that no one can find out anything about what comes after.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[15] In my fleeting days I have seen it all: a righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[16] Do not be excessively righteous, and do not make yourself overly wise. Why destroy yourself?
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[17] Do not be excessively wicked, and do not be a fool. Why die before your time?
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[18] It is good to grasp the one and not let go of the other, for whoever fears God will come through with both.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[19] Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers in a city.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[20] Surely there is no one on earth so righteous that he does good and never sins.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[21] Do not take to heart every word people say, or you may hear your servant cursing you.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[22] For your own heart knows how many times you yourself have cursed others.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[23] All this I tested with wisdom. I said, "I will be wise"—but it was far from me.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[24] Whatever exists is far off and deep, very deep. Who can discover it?
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[25] I turned my heart to know and explore and seek out wisdom and the reason of things, and to know that wickedness is folly and that folly is madness.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[26] And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net and whose hands are chains. The one who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner she captures.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[27] See, this is what I found, says the Preacher, adding one thing to another to find the sum:
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[28] What my soul kept searching for I did not find: one man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I did not find.
[Ecclesiastes] [7]:[29] This alone I found: God made mankind upright, but they have gone in search of many schemes.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[1] Who is like the wise? Who knows how to interpret a thing? Wisdom lights up a person's face and softens the hardness of his features.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[2] I say: keep the king's command, because of the oath sworn before God.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[3] Do not be quick to leave his presence, and do not persist in a bad cause, for he does whatever he pleases.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[4] The king's word carries authority, and who can say to him, "What are you doing?"
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[5] Whoever keeps the command will meet no harm, and a wise heart knows the right time and the right verdict.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[6] For every matter has its time and its verdict, though a person's trouble weighs heavily on him.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[7] For no one knows what is coming; who can tell him how it will be?
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[8] No one has power over the wind, to hold it back — no one has power over the day of death. There is no discharge in war, and wickedness will not save the one who practices it.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[9] All this I saw, as I set my mind on every deed done under the sun: a time when one person rules over another to that person's harm.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[10] And so I saw the wicked buried — they used to come and go from the holy place, and they were forgotten in the city where they had done such things. This too is vanity.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[11] Because the sentence for an evil deed is not carried out quickly, the human heart is filled with the urge to do wrong.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[12] Though the sinner does evil a hundred times and still lives long, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, who stand in awe before him.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[13] But it will not be well with the wicked; his days will not stretch out like a lengthening shadow, because he does not fear God.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[14] There is a vanity that happens on the earth: there are righteous people who receive what the deeds of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked people who receive what the deeds of the righteous deserve. I said that this too is vanity.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[15] So I commended joy, since there is nothing better for a person under the sun than to eat and drink and be glad. This will go with him in his toil through the days of the life God has given him under the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[16] When I set my mind to know wisdom and to see the business that goes on upon the earth — how a man's eyes see no sleep, day or night —
[Ecclesiastes] [8]:[17] then I saw all the work of God: that no one can grasp the work that is done under the sun. However hard a person labors to search it out, he will not find it; and even if the wise claim to know, they cannot find it.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[1] All this I took to heart, examining it closely: that the righteous and the wise and all they do are in God's hand. No one knows whether love or hate awaits him; everything lies before them.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[2] The same fate comes to everyone alike: to the righteous and the wicked, to the good, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. As it goes for the good, so for the sinner; as for the one who swears an oath, so for the one who fears to swear.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[3] This is an evil in everything done under the sun: one fate comes to all. And the hearts of men are full of evil, and madness fills their hearts while they live, and afterward they go to the dead.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[4] But whoever is among the living still has hope; a living dog is better than a dead lion.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[5] The living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing; they have no more reward, for their memory is forgotten.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[6] Their love, their hate, their jealousy—all of it has already perished, and never again will they have a share in anything done under the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[7] Go, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a glad heart, for God has already approved what you do.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[8] Let your clothes always be white, and never lack oil on your head.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[9] Enjoy life with the wife you love, all the fleeting days of life that God has given you under the sun—all your fleeting days. For this is your portion in life and in the work you toil at under the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[10] Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your strength, for there is no work or planning, no knowledge or wisdom, in the grave where you are going.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[11] Again I saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor wealth to the discerning, nor favor to the skilled; for time and chance overtake them all.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[12] For no one even knows his own hour. Like fish caught in a cruel net, like birds trapped in a snare, so are people ensnared at a time of disaster, when it falls upon them without warning.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[13] I also saw this instance of wisdom under the sun, and it made a deep impression on me.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[14] There was a small city with only a few people in it, and a great king came against it, surrounded it, and built massive siegeworks against it.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[15] Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and by his wisdom he saved the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[16] So I said: Wisdom is better than strength. Yet the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and no one listens to his words.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[17] The quiet words of the wise are heard above the shouting of a ruler of fools.
[Ecclesiastes] [9]:[18] Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner can destroy much good.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[1] Dead flies make the perfumer's oil stink and ferment; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[2] The heart of the wise inclines to the right, but the heart of the fool to the left.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[3] Even on the road, when the fool walks, his sense fails him, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[4] If the ruler's temper flares against you, do not leave your post, for composure lays great offenses to rest.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[5] There is an evil I have seen under the sun, the kind of error that comes from a ruler:
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[6] folly is set in many high places, while the rich sit in low places.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[7] I have seen slaves on horseback, and princes walking on foot like slaves.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[8] Whoever digs a pit may fall into it, and whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[9] Whoever quarries stones may be hurt by them, and whoever splits logs is endangered by them.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[10] If the axe is dull and its edge is not sharpened, more strength must be used; but the advantage of wisdom is that it brings success.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[11] If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[12] The words of a wise man's mouth win favor, but the lips of a fool consume him.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[13] His words begin in folly and end in wicked madness.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[14] Yet the fool multiplies words. No one knows what is coming, and who can tell anyone what will happen after him?
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[15] The toil of fools wears them out, for they do not even know the way to town.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[16] Woe to you, O land, whose king is a boy and whose princes feast in the morning.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[17] Blessed are you, O land, whose king is nobly born and whose princes feast at the proper time—for strength, and not for drunkenness.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[18] Through sloth the roof sags, and through idle hands the house leaks.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[19] Bread is made for laughter, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.
[Ecclesiastes] [10]:[20] Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, and do not curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your voice, and some winged creature may report your words.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[1] Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[2] Give a portion to seven, or even to eight, for you do not know what disaster may come upon the earth.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[3] When the clouds are full, they empty their rain on the earth; and whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, wherever it falls, there it lies.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[4] Whoever watches the wind will never sow, and whoever studies the clouds will never reap.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[5] Just as you do not know the way of the wind, or how bones are formed in a mother's womb, so you cannot know the work of God, who makes all things.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[6] Sow your seed in the morning, and in the evening do not let your hand rest, for you do not know which will succeed, this one or that, or whether both alike will do well.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[7] Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[8] However many years anyone may live, let them rejoice in them all; but let them remember the days of darkness, for there will be many. Everything that comes is fleeting.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[9] Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart be glad in the days of your prime. Follow the ways of your heart and whatever your eyes see, but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
[Ecclesiastes] [11]:[10] So banish vexation from your heart and put away trouble from your body, for youth and the dawn of life are fleeting.
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[1] Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years arrive when you will say, "I find no pleasure in them";
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[2] before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain;
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[3] when the guards of the house tremble and the strong men are bent, when the grinding women stop because they are few, and those who look through the windows grow dim;
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[4] when the doors to the street are shut and the sound of the mill fades low, when one rises at the sound of a bird and all the daughters of song grow faint;
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[5] when they are afraid of heights and terrors lie in the road; when the almond tree blossoms and the grasshopper drags itself along and desire fails. For a man goes to his eternal home, and the mourners walk about in the street;
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[6] before the silver cord snaps and the golden bowl is shattered, before the jar is broken at the spring and the wheel is smashed at the well,
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[7] and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[8] Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity.
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[9] Moreover, because the Preacher was wise, he kept on teaching the people knowledge; he weighed and searched out and arranged many proverbs.
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[10] The Preacher sought to find pleasing words, and what he wrote was upright—words of truth.
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[11] The words of the wise are like goads, and collected sayings like nails firmly driven; all are given by one Shepherd.
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[12] As for anything beyond these, my son, be warned: the making of many books has no end, and much study wearies the body.
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[13] The end of the matter, now that all has been heard: fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
[Ecclesiastes] [12]:[14] For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[1] The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[2] Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth—for your love is better than wine.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[3] The fragrance of your oils is sweet; your name is oil poured out—therefore the maidens love you.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[4] Take me with you—let us run! The king has brought me into his chambers. We will rejoice and be glad in you; we will praise your love more than wine. Rightly do they love you.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[5] I am dark, and I am lovely, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[6] Do not stare at me because I am dark, because the sun has gazed upon me. My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[7] Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where do you pasture your flock, where do you let it rest at noon? Why should I be like a veiled woman beside the flocks of your companions?
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[8] If you do not know, most beautiful of women, follow the tracks of the flock and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[9] I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[10] Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[11] We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[12] While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[13] My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh, resting all night between my breasts.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[14] My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[15] How beautiful you are, my love, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are doves.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[16] How handsome you are, my beloved, how delightful! And our bed is lush and green.
[Song of Solomon] [1]:[17] The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are cypress.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[1] I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys.[^1] [^1]: The Hebrew flower names are uncertain; the first may be a crocus or meadow flower, the second a lotus or lily.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[2] Like a lily among thorns is my darling among the young women.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[3] Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest is my beloved among the young men. I delight to sit in his shade, and his fruit is sweet to my taste.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[4] He brought me to the banquet hall, and his banner over me is love.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[5] Sustain me with raisin cakes, refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[6] His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[7] I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the does of the field: do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[8] The voice of my beloved! Look, here he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[9] My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Look, there he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, peering through the lattice.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[10] My beloved spoke and said to me: Rise up, my darling, my beautiful one, and come away.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[11] For see, the winter is past; the rains are over and gone.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[12] The blossoms appear in the land, the season of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.[^1] [^1]: The Hebrew word may mean either "singing" or "pruning".
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[13] The fig tree ripens its early fruit, and the blossoming vines give off their fragrance. Rise up, my darling, my beautiful one, and come away.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[14] My dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding places of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[15] Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[16] My beloved is mine and I am his; he grazes among the lilies.
[Song of Solomon] [2]:[17] Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the cleft mountains.
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[1] On my bed through the nights I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but I did not find him.
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[2] Let me rise now and go about the city, through the streets and the squares; let me seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I did not find him.
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[3] The watchmen found me as they made their rounds in the city. "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?"
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[4] Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him and would not let him go until I had brought him to my mother's house, to the room of her who conceived me.
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[5] I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and by the does of the field: do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[6] Who is this coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of the merchant?
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[7] Look—Solomon's couch, with sixty warriors around it, from the mighty men of Israel,
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[8] all of them wielding the sword, trained for battle, each with his sword at his side against the terrors of the night.
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[9] King Solomon made himself a palanquin from the wood of Lebanon.[fn]
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[10] Its posts he made of silver, its base of gold, its seat of purple; its interior inlaid with love from the daughters of Jerusalem.
[Song of Solomon] [3]:[11] Come out, daughters of Zion, and gaze on King Solomon, wearing the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day his heart rejoiced.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[1] How beautiful you are, my love, how beautiful! Your eyes behind your veil are doves. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down the slopes of Gilead.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[2] Your teeth are like a flock of newly shorn ewes coming up from the washing, each one bearing twins, and none of them bereaved.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[3] Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Your cheek behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[4] Your neck is like the tower of David, built in courses of stone;[^1] a thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of warriors. [^1]: The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain; it may refer to rows of stonework or to an armory.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[5] Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[6] Until the day grows cool and the shadows flee, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[7] You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[8] Come with me from Lebanon, my bride, with me from Lebanon. Look down from the peak of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountain haunts of leopards.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[9] You have stolen my heart, my sister, my bride; you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your necklace.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[10] How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than any spice!
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[11] Your lips drip nectar, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the scent of your garments is like the scent of Lebanon.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[12] A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring enclosed, a sealed fountain.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[13] Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates with choicest fruits, henna with nard,
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[14] nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with every tree of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all the finest spices.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[15] You are a garden fountain, a well of living water, streams flowing down from Lebanon.
[Song of Solomon] [4]:[16] Awake, north wind, and come, south wind! Blow upon my garden, that its spices may flow. Let my beloved come to his garden and eat its choicest fruits.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[1] I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have gathered my myrrh with my spices, eaten my honeycomb with my honey, drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends; drink, and drink deeply, lovers.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[2] I was asleep, but my heart was awake. Listen — my beloved is knocking: "Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my flawless one; my head is drenched with dew, my hair with the damp of the night."
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[3] I have taken off my robe — must I put it on again? I have washed my feet — must I soil them?
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[4] My beloved reached his hand through the opening, and my inmost being yearned for him.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[5] I rose to open to my beloved, and my hands were dripping with myrrh, my fingers with flowing myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[6] I opened to my beloved, but he had turned away and gone. My soul went out to him as he spoke. I looked for him and did not find him; I called him, and he gave no answer.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[7] The watchmen making their rounds in the city found me. They struck me, they wounded me; the guards of the walls stripped away my cloak.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[8] I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him this — that I am faint with love.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[9] What sets your beloved above others, most beautiful of women? What sets your beloved above others, that you charge us so?
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[10] My beloved is radiant and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[11] His head is purest gold; his hair is wavy and black as a raven.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[12] His eyes are like doves beside the streams of water, washed in milk, resting where the waters brim.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[13] His cheeks are like beds of spice, banks of fragrant blossoms; his lips are lilies dripping with flowing myrrh.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[14] His arms are rods of gold set with topaz; his body is polished ivory adorned with sapphires.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[15] His legs are pillars of marble set on bases of gold. His bearing is like Lebanon, majestic as the cedars.
[Song of Solomon] [5]:[16] His mouth is sweetness itself; he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved, this is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.
[Song of Solomon] [6]:[1] Where has your beloved gone, most beautiful of women? Which way has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?
[Song of Solomon] [6]:[2] My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies.
[Song of Solomon] [6]:[3] I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.
[Song of Solomon] [6]:[4] You are as beautiful as Tirzah, my love, as lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.

[Song of Solomon] [6]:[6] Your teeth are like a flock of ewes coming up from the washing, each one bearing twins, and not one among them bereaved.
[Song of Solomon] [6]:[7] Your cheek behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate.
